hook: We can predict where a parabola lands. But what if it changes course halfway?

do_not_include: guidance algorithms, materials, interceptor performance comparisons
include_only: why a ballistic path is predictable
how Earth's curvature limits radar line of sight

concepts.ballistic: After the boost phase the engine shuts off and only inertia and gravity act, so the path is essentially fixed; knowing the position and velocity at engine cutoff gives the landing point.
concepts.glide: Instead of falling straight back down after the boost, the vehicle glides on lift in the upper atmosphere and can change direction, so its path is no longer one fixed parabola.
concepts.near_space: Near space is roughly 20 to 100 km up; in plain language, it sits between traditional air defense and the space layer.
concepts.radar_horizon: The Earth is round, so a radar's line of sight is limited by curvature; the lower and later a target appears, the less warning time there is.
why_hard: Seen late: a low glide is detected later than a high arc
Hard to reach: near space, roughly 20 to 100 km, is a gap between traditional defenses
Hard to predict: it can maneuver, so the predicted meeting point fails

metaphors.note: 'Skipping stone' and 'gap' are metaphors, not literal physical processes; the picture is labeled schematic, not to scale
metaphors.skipping: Gliding 'like a skipping stone' is a metaphor for lift-assisted gliding, not literal bouncing off the atmosphere

publish.cover_text: SEEN LATE · HARD TO REACH · HARD TO PREDICT
publish.title: Why can't some trajectories be predicted? Qian Xuesen saw it 70 years ago
publish.description: Last episode: a parabola's landing point can be calculated. This one: why sometimes it can't. Public physics principles and history only. Engine off means only inertia and gravity act, so the path is fixed; glide on lift and change direction, and it isn't. Schematic, not to scale, no real parameters, no specific missiles. Next: pendulum or light refraction? Tell us in the comments.

shots.口播: A ballistic missile is basically a thrown stone. The rocket boosts it up, the engine shuts off, and only inertia and gravity are left. The path is fixed: see the first half on radar, and you can work out the rest.
shots.字幕: Engine off: only inertia and gravity. The path is fixed.
shots.画面: Globe + ballistic arc: boost, engine-cutoff marker, then gravity only; code panel reuses EP01's x(t), y(t); chapter stamp: ENGINE OFF: INERTIA + GRAVITY; 01 checked

shots.口播: Over seventy years ago, Qian Xuesen proposed a new idea: don't just fall back down. Use lift in the upper atmosphere to glide, a bit like a skipping stone, and even change direction.
shots.字幕: Don't fall back down. Glide on lift.
shots.画面: Same globe; the trajectory enters a glide at altitude, lift arrow up, one turn; subtitle note: skipping stone is a metaphor, schematic not to scale; stamp: DON'T DIVE. GLIDE ON LIFT.; 02 checked

shots.口播: Problem one: it's seen late. The Earth is round, so radar can't see past the horizon. Glide low, and it shows up late, leaving less time to react.
shots.字幕: Seen late: glide low, show up late.
shots.画面: Earth curvature + radar beam + blind zone: the high arc is seen first, the low glide later; sub-chapter stamp: SEEN LATE

shots.口播: Problem two: hard to reach. Near space, about 20 to 100 kilometers up, sits between traditional air defense and the space layer, awkward for both.
shots.字幕: Hard to reach: near space is a gap.
shots.画面: Layers: traditional air defense below, space above, near space (about 20-100 km) highlighted in between, glide path inside it; sub-chapter stamp: HARD TO REACH

shots.口播: Problem three: it's hard to predict. Interception needs a predicted meeting point, but it can turn, so that point fails, and you have to keep recalculating.
shots.字幕: Hard to predict: it turns, the prediction fails.
shots.画面: The glide turns midway, the earlier predicted meeting point is crossed out, a new one appears; sub-chapter stamp: HARD TO PREDICT; 03 checked

shots.口播: No fixed parabola, no easy math. Next: pendulum or refraction?
